plain_english: A shallow person never looks to himself for help or harm. He only looks to outside things. A philosopher looks to himself for all help or harm.
original_excerpt: The condition and characteristic of a vulgar person is that he never looks for either help or harm from himself, but only from externals. The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is that he looks to himself for all help or harm.

plain_english: A skilled person doesn't criticize anyone, praise anyone, blame anyone, or accuse anyone. They don't talk about themselves like they're important or know everything. When something blocks or stops them, they blame themselves. If someone praises them, they quietly smile to themselves. If someone criticizes them, they don't defend themselves. They move through life like someone recovering from illness — careful not to mess with anything that's going well but still fragile. They hold back their desires. They only avoid things that interfere with how they use their own will. They use their energy carefully in everything. If they look stupid or ignorant, they don't care. In short, they watch themselves like they're watching an enemy in hiding.
original_excerpt: The marks of a proficient are that he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one; says nothing concerning himself as being anybody or knowing anything. When he is in any instance hindered or restrained, he accuses himself; and if he is praised, he smiles to himself at the person who praises him; and if he is censured, he makes no defense. But he goes about with the caution of a convalescent, careful of interference with anything that is doing well but not yet quite secure. He restrains desire; he transfers his aversion to those things only which thwart the proper use of our own will; he employs his energies moderately in all directions; if he appears stupid or ignorant, he does not care; and, in a word, he keeps watch over himself as over an enemy and one in ambush.
